newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Klima says Bank Austria controversy damaging.
newsitem.headline: Klima says Bank Austria controversy damaging.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima, rejecting accusations he had hushed up a controversial banking deal, said on Thursday that a heated debate around Bank Austria's privatisation was hurting the nation's reputation.

Klima was speaking at the beginning of an extraordinary parliamentary session, called by the far-right Freedom Party. The debate should cast light on when the government learned Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale had acquired first refusal on a majority stake in state-owned Bank Austria.

Klima's Social Democrats stand accused of backing Bank Austria's acquisition of rival Creditanstalt in January in the knowledge that WestLB already had first option on Vienna's 45.15 percent Bank Austria voting stake. Social Democrats dominate Vienna city hall.

"It is remarkable how leading Social Democrats presented the Bank Austria-Creditanstalt deal as a great Austrian solution while knowing that the eventual sale of both to a foreign bank was on the cards," the Freedom Party said.
Klima, who was due to fly to Sweden later on Thursday, insisted he was ignorant of the first refusal deal, struck in 1995 between Vienna City holding company AVZ and WestLB.
"I was not informed," Klima told deputies, adding: "This search for scapegoats is damaging to Austria's banks and economy."

Opposition parties and coalition partner the People's Party have expressed outrage that Social Democrat politicians, including Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl and Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger kept quiet about the WestLB agreement.

Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner, a member of the conservative People's Party, has called on the government to annul Creditanstalt's privatisation if WestLB insists on maintaining its first refusal.
"The coalition parties have succeeded in building up mutual trust in recent months. The last thing we want is to lose that trust," Farnleitner said.

A division over Creditanstalt's six-year privatisation brought the coalition government to the brink of collapse at the start of the year. Then the People's Party only agreed reluctantly to allow Social Democrat-dominated Bank Austria to take over the country's most conservative bank.

Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa, who as an AVZ board member played an instrumental role in the WestLB deal, echoed Klima's warning. The bank was expected to announce the share price for three billion schillings capital increase later on Thursday.
"I have the impression there is a deliberate attempt to do us damage," Randa said, adding that the very public dispute threatened to undermine investor confidence.
Analysts said the preference share issue should be a success based on purely financial data but noted political disputes over Austria's closed banking sector tended to distract from fundamentals.
Bank Austria preferred shares were trading 8.5 schillings down at 415.5 at midday in a flat Vienna market.
